p26: 26.  In 1991 and 1998 the Language Association, a non-governmental organisation, published two dictionaries entitled “Turkish Dictionary for Pupils” (Öğrenciler için Türkçe Sözlük) and “Turkish Dictionary” (Türkçe Sözlük) respectively. The publication of these dictionaries was partly funded by the Ministry of Culture.
p27: 27.  On 30 April 2002 the applicant, acting on behalf of the Confederation of Roma/Gypsy Cultural Associations, sent a letter to the executive board of the Language Association in which he argued that certain entries in the dictionaries were insulting and discriminatory towards Roma/Gypsies.
p28: 28.  On page 279 of both dictionaries, the following entries appeared in respect of the term “Gypsy” (çingene)
p29: 29.  In the applicant’s view, the entries concerning the Gypsy community were negative, discriminatory and prejudiced. He further asserted that the Ministry of Education and the Turkish Academy had amended their dictionaries at his request, and he called on the Language Association likewise to rectify the above-mentioned definitions and to remove all discriminatory expressions from the dictionaries. He did not receive a reply.
p30: 30.  Subsequently, on 15 July 2002, the applicant sent a further letter to the Language Association, in which he reiterated his request and stated that he would bring proceedings against the association if he did not obtain satisfaction by 20 August 2002.
p31: 31.  On 16 April 2003 the applicant brought an action against the Language Association in the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance (*tribunal de grande instance d’Ankara*), requesting that the above-mentioned definitions and expressions be removed from the dictionaries. He also sought compensation for the non-pecuniary damage he claimed to have sustained as a result of the expressions in question, which in his view amounted to an attack on his Gypsy identity and an insult to him personally.
p32: 32.  The Language Association filed observations in reply in which it argued, in particular, that the definitions and expressions in the dictionaries were based on historical and sociological reality and did not reflect any intention to humiliate or debase an ethnic group. It added that the expressions and definitions in question were in common use in society and that there were other similar expressions in the Turkish language concerning Albanians, Jews and the Turks themselves.
p33: 33.  On 16 July 2003 the Ankara Civil Court of First Instance (*tribunal de grande instance d’Ankara*) dismissed the applicant’s claims. It held that the definitions and expressions in the dictionaries were based on historical and sociological reality and did not reflect any intention to humiliate or debase an ethnic group. It further noted that there were similar expressions in the Turkish language concerning other ethnic groups, which appeared in dictionaries and encyclopaedias.
p34: 34.  The applicant appealed against that decision to the Court of Cassation (*Cour de cassation*), which upheld it on 15 March 2004.
